newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan stocks not responding to reform - report.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan stocks not responding to reform - report.

text.p: Pakistani bourses are not responding well to reforms launched by the caretaker government in the last few weeks, according to a report by brokerage house Khadim Ali Shah Bukhari Ltd (KASB).
"Markets failed to fully embrace the stock exchange package announced this week, the apparent thawing of relations with IMF, or any other good news," KASB said in the report.

The government has cut duties, liberalised import of textile processing machinery, withdrawn a five percent customs duty on imported cotton and slashed regulatory duties on polyester fibre imports to help the ailing textile sector.

It also unveiled a stock market package last week that included removing 10 percent withholding tax on bonus shares, exempting insurance companies from capital gains tax and allowing repurchase of up to 10 percent of treasury stocks.

"We are particularly optimistic on the long-term impact of these measures for insurance companies and mutual funds," KASB said. "However, we caution that institutions (including insurance companies) would take advantage to prune portfolios thereby instigating bouts of selling pressure."

KASB said the markets had not been won over by the efforts of Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to Prime Minister Meraj Khalid, to revive a stalled $600 million standby loan from the International Monetary Fund.
Burki is now in Washington to start talks on a longer-term programme known as an enhanced structural adjustment facility.

Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, sacked by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, has said the caretaker government had no legal right to enter into a long-term agreement with the IMF.

"Uncertainty and instability created by Benazir's posture, bomb blasts, question-marks over the continuity of policies post-election and the future political climate are dissuading investors from entering the market," the report said.
"While the rain of packages attempts to shoot confidece into investors, political uncertainty surrounding post-February 3 continues to divide opinions and sabotage sentiments.

"Having said that, we feel that the market's uncertainty, characterised by volatile swings around a flat trend line, could well be the order of the day (month) until the national elections," the report concluded.
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index fell 14.72 points, or one percent, to end at 1,460.58 on Thursday, compared with 1,492.37 a week earlier, and opened lower on Sunday.
KASB said market capitalisation fell to $11 billion last week from $11.03 billion a week before.
